Autosomal recessive — mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4

● Family History: ​Hematuria, renal disease, urolithiasis, sickle cell anemia, bleeding disorders,\nhemophilia, deafness (Alport's syndrome), hypertension.

qs.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of Alport’s syndrome (hereditary nephritis)?
o: C. Marked hypotension and salt-wasting nephropathy
A. High-frequency hearing loss without deafness
D. Complete absence of hematuria throughout
B. Conductive hearing loss with profound deafness
qs.e: Alport’s syndrome is a congenital defect of collagen presenting with hematuria, pyuria, proteinuria, high-frequency hearing loss without deafness, and visual disturbances. It progresses to renal failure without effective curative treatment.

qs.q: A 20-year-old male with Alport syndrome undergoes a kidney transplant. What specific complication is he at increased risk of developing post-transplant?
o: Immediate hyperacute rejection due to ABO incompatibility
Recurrent Alport syndrome in the donor kidney
Anti-GBM nephritis due to recognition of normal donor collagen
qs.e: Patients with Alport syndrome may develop anti-GBM nephritis after transplantation because their immune system recognizes the normal type IV collagen in the donor kidney as foreign. The disease does not recur in the donor kidney because the donor has normal genes.

qs.q: A patient with Alport syndrome has a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. What is the most common mode of inheritance for this specific genetic variant?
qs.e: Mutations in the COL4A5 gene cause the most common form of Alport syndrome, which is X-linked (~80% of cases). COL4A3 and COL4A4 mutations are associated with autosomal recessive or dominant forms.

ai.title: Alport Syndrome
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A hereditary nephritis due to type IV collagen mutations, presenting with hematuria, progressive renal failure, sensorineural deafness and ocular changes. Diagnosis relies on family history, urinalysis, audiology and renal biopsy when available.

sections.p: Alport syndrome is an inherited defect of type IV collagen (COL4A5 X‑linked, COL4A3/4 autosomal). It causes a characteristic triad of hematuria, sensorineural deafness and ocular changes. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by urinalysis, audiometry and, if possible, renal biopsy showing GBM thinning and splitting.

t.b: Detects persistent microscopic hematuria; a result of glomerular bleeding
Identifies sensorineural hearing loss; confirms the classic feature
Shows GBM thinning, splitting and lamellation; rules out immune complex disease

sections.p: Renal disease is staged by eGFR and proteinuria. Early stages: isolated hematuria. Stage 3–4: proteinuria >1 g/day, declining eGFR. Stage 5: end‑stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplant.

t.b: Estimates renal function; a decline >10 ml/min/1.73 m² per year indicates progression

sections.p: Genetic mutations in COL4A5 (X‑linked) are the primary cause. In low‑resource settings, secondary causes of hematuria (e.g., urinary tract infection, schistosomiasis) must be excluded first.

t.b: Positive for hematuria, renal failure or deafness in relatives

sections.p: Children often have painless gross or microscopic hematuria. Deafness may appear in early childhood. Ocular findings (posterior lenticonus, anterior lenticonus) are less common but important. Renal failure usually manifests after adolescence.
Key tests are urinalysis, renal ultrasound, audiometry and, if feasible, renal biopsy. In resource‑poor settings, a simple dipstick and basic renal function tests guide management.

t.b: Confirms presence of blood; persistent positivity suggests glomerular source
Monitors renal function; rising levels indicate progression

sections.p: Rapid decline in eGFR, hypertension, severe proteinuria, sudden hearing loss or visual changes require urgent referral. Complications include ESRD, hypertension, and hearing loss progression.

Supportive care: ACE inhibitors or ARBs for proteinuria and hypertension; avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast). Audiological rehabilitation and regular eye exams. Prepare for renal replacement therapy when eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m².
Annual review of renal function, blood pressure, hearing and vision. Genetic counselling for families. No specific prevention; early detection allows timely intervention.
Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria), IgA nephropathy, post‑streptococcal GN, and Goodpasture’s syndrome.
b: Thin basement membrane disease – isolated hematuria

sections.p: Normal serum creatinine can mask early renal impairment; dipstick may miss microhematuria; audiometry may be unavailable, delaying diagnosis.

t.b: May remain normal until significant loss of function

faq.q: Why is Alport syndrome usually X‑linked?
faq.a: Most pathogenic mutations are in COL4A5 on the X chromosome, explaining the male predominance.

faq.q: Can a child with Alport have normal hearing?
faq.a: Yes, hearing loss may appear later; some patients remain normal into adulthood.

faq.q: What is the role of ACE inhibitors?
faq.a: They reduce proteinuria and slow progression of renal failure by lowering intraglomerular pressure.

exam: A 10‑year‑old boy presents with painless hematuria and a family history of kidney failure in his father. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Alport syndrome, supported by family history and hematuria.
You suspect Alport syndrome but the patient has normal serum creatinine. What next? — Perform urinalysis for hematuria and proteinuria, audiometry, and consider renal ultrasound.
A patient with Alport syndrome develops sudden hearing loss. What is the immediate management? — Refer to audiology for hearing aids and start ACE inhibitor if proteinuria present.
Which investigation is most definitive for Alport syndrome? — Renal biopsy showing GBM thinning and splitting.
Why are NSAIDs contraindicated in Alport syndrome? — They can worsen renal function by reducing renal perfusion.
A patient with Alport syndrome is on an ACE inhibitor but develops cough. What is the alternative? — Switch to an ARB.
